Data in, data out

What the model is actually handed, and what it actually gives back, at every stage, with the real numbers rather than a sketch of them. Every word that could send you to a glossary is explained where it appears.

  • 1 One cell, written out
  • 2 What goes in
  • 3 What the model does
  • 4 What comes out
  • 5 What you get back, and what you don't

1One cell, written out

A cell is one square of the city — 1.2 km on a side — and it is one training example. The model sees a whole cell at once.

Cut that square into a 1024 × 1024 chequerboard. Each little square is a unit: 1.17 m of ground, about the width of a doorway. For every unit we work out 6 numbers, one per indicator. Those 6 numbers are the unit's vector.

one unit, at row 470, column 300: [1.00, 0.58, 10.98, 13.95, 1.04, 0.04] building_binary · building_density · accessibility_gravity poi_count · poi_entropy · road_density

Now take one indicator at a time and lay its number for every unit back onto the chequerboard. That sheet is a grid. Here is a 4 × 4 corner of the building-density grid, so you can see it is just numbers in a square:

0.58 0.58 0.57 0.57 0.58 0.57 0.57 0.57 0.58 0.57 0.57 0.57 0.57 0.57 0.57 0.56

Stack the 6 grids and you have the whole cell. Two ways of writing the same thing, and both are correct — it is the same numbers either way:

as 6 sheets, each 1024 × 1024: shape (6, 1024, 1024) as a 1024 × 1024 board, each square holding 6 numbers: shape (1024, 1024, 6) a 2 × 2 corner, written the second way: [ 1.00, 0.58, 10.98, 13.95, 1.04, 0.04] [ 1.00, 0.58, 11.01, 13.97, 1.03, 0.04] [ 1.00, 0.58, 10.95, 13.94, 1.04, 0.04] [ 1.00, 0.57, 10.98, 13.95, 1.04, 0.04] either way: 6,291,456 numbers in one cell.

The word tensor just means this stack. It is not a special kind of object; it is the pile of grids.

2What goes in

One thing happens to a cell before the model sees it, and it is arithmetic, not interpretation.

Standardizing. For each grid separately: work out the average of all its numbers, subtract that average from every number, then divide every number by how spread out they were.

Afterwards that grid's numbers centre on zero and have a spread of one. The picture is unchanged — the bright parts are still bright. Only the numbers on them are different.

Why bother: the grids arrive in wildly different units. Building density runs 0 to 1. Shop counts run 0 to 60. Left alone, the shop grid's numbers are sixty times bigger, and anything that measures distance would be listening almost entirely to shops. Standardizing gives every grid the same say.

Everything needed to undo it — the average and the spread, per grid — is written down and kept. That stored pair is the decoder. Nothing else is needed to get back.

3What the model does

A diffusion model has two halves, and only one of them learns anything.

The noise recipe. Fixed, written down in advance, no learning. It says how much random noise to mix into a cell at each of 1000 steps, until nothing of the original is left.

The network. Shown a noisy cell, it guesses what noise is in it. This is the part that is trained, by showing it noisy cells and correcting its guesses, over and over.

To generate, you run the recipe backwards. Start from pure noise, ask the network what noise it sees, subtract a bit of its answer, repeat about a thousand times. What is left is a new cell.

Nothing in that loop checks whether the network is any good. It asks, it subtracts, it moves on. So an untrained network — one whose numbers are still the random values it was created with, never trained on anything — produces output perfectly happily. The output is just nonsense.

That last figure is also why we bother measuring what an untrained model scores. If nonsense scores 0.05 on a test, then a trained model scoring 0.05 has not achieved anything either. It is a "do not get excited below this line" mark.

4What comes out

The model gives back exactly the shape it was given: 6 grids, 1024 × 1024. It is never reshaped, at any point, going in or coming out.

But the numbers are in the standardized form — centred on zero, spread of one — so they mean nothing physically yet. Unpacking fixes that, and it is the standardizing run backwards:

Unpacking. For each grid: multiply every number by the spread we stored, then add back the average we stored.

That is the entire operation. It is exact, it costs nothing, and it cannot be wrong, because it is the same arithmetic that got us here.

Unpacking does not check anything. The demo above was trained for eight seconds on eight cells, so its output is nowhere near real data — and unpacking dutifully turns that into −705 shops within 300 m.

A negative shop count is impossible. Unpacking will produce it anyway, because its job is to undo arithmetic, not to judge. Sanity of the numbers is a separate question, asked afterwards.

5What you get back, and what you don't

You get back: 6 named grids of numbers in real units — share of ground built on, shops within 300 m, bits of mixedness, metres of street per square metre. You can look at them, measure them, compare them against real cells, map them.

You do not get back: buildings, roads or shops as shapes. There is no address anywhere in a generated cell. A grid says "this patch scores 0.58 on building density" and nothing more — not which building, not where its walls are.

This is a deliberate choice rather than a limitation we ran into. Turning grids back into shapes would need a second trained model to do the translating, and then any near-copy we detected might be an artefact of that second model rather than a fact about the first. Keeping the encoding a written rule keeps the way back free and beyond argument.

So: the stack of grids is what the model reads and what it writes. Standardizing and unpacking move the numbers between measured units and model units. Nothing is ever reshaped, and nothing is ever recovered that was not put in.
